body.text: When Rodrigo Duterte takes the stand before the world criminal court next week, he will do so as the first former Asian leader to be tried at The Hague.

The significance of the moment is not lost on those afflicted by his years-long anti-drug campaign that led to thousands of extra-judicial killings in the Philippines — many of whom are hoping to give evidence at the International Criminal Court (ICC) when his trial begins on Monday.

The case has several implications — including how leaders from countries such as the Philippines can still be held accountable even after withdrawing from the court's jurisdiction, and the court's ability to consider alleged crimes committed in a domestic crackdown.
But some are concerned it may be one of the last such trials at the ICC.

The United States' vow to dismantle the court "brick by brick" has put unprecedented pressure on its functions and viability. The US has imposed extraordinary sanctions on judges and the court itself in an attempt to strip its basic functioning abilities.
"The sanctions are there to make the ICC's job a living hell," Tamer Morris, an international law expert at the University of Sydney, told SBS News.
Such is the pressure, many are beginning to ask the question whether there will soon be a court left.
Why is the US seeking to end the ICC?
The Trump administration sanctions are aimed at punishing the court over fears US soldiers could be prosecuted on foreign soil. But it's also about another controversial issue.
"It is (about) protecting their friends," Morris said.
He said when the sanctions were first announced, US President Donald Trump pointed to the ICC's arrest warrants against Israeli leaders Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, as a reason for them.

"I think the argument of protecting their soldiers is a bit of a false argument or a political domestic argument. It really is more kind of trying to protect their friends, specifically the recent response against Netanyahu," Morris said.

The US is not a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that governs the court's jurisdiction over signatory countries, of which there are 125. The ICC only has jurisdiction over conduct which is committed in the territory of a state party.
International law expert Juliette McIntyre from Adelaide University says the US argument of protecting its soldiers is not legitimate.

"Provided that US citizens are not going around committing war crimes in the territory of any state party to the Rome Statute, then there's no basis for being concerned about the ICC exercising jurisdiction over its citizens," she told SBS News.
"So what business does it have dismantling an international organisation that other states have decided to set up?
"This is a very explicit attempt to shield wrongdoers from facing the consequences of their actions."
Can the US succeed in dismantling the court?

Over the past year, the US has sanctioned judges, chief and deputy prosecutors and the court itself — impacting its receipt of money, accessing services and conducting transactions in the US and preventing officials' travel to the US.
Its deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan recently told SBS News she was unable to hold a credit card, her family was also impacted, and she was concerned about service disruptions.
"We are not cowed," she said. "We are determined to carry on."

Rights monitors have noted the court has had to swap email providers from Microsoft to a European brand, change insurance, avoid official dealings with US citizens, companies or currency, and pay staff in advance.
"The demands that the US is making are simply beyond the pale," McIntyre said.
The Trump administration is also pressuring other countries (under the threat of retribution) to withdraw from the Rome Statute.

So far, seven countries — including Niger, Venezuela and Nauru — have started the process of withdrawal. (Tajikistan started the process after facing criticism from the ICC over its failure to arrest Russian president Vladimir Putin during a visit in 2025).
Tamer says this is what could ultimately lead to the court's dismantling.
"The power of the court's jurisdiction is having more signatories, having more states aligned to it, and so having states slowly withdraw one by one is going to probably be its ending."
Australia, a signatory, has so far resisted US pressure and remains party to the Statute.

Asked whether the trial of Duterte — who rights groups described as a "dictator" and who is facing charges of crimes against humanity — may be the court's final such trial, Morris said: "It could be. I don't think it will be. But they are starting to go down that road."
What will happen to the criminal court?
It could become a symbolic court.

If the court survives, one alternative scenario in the face of a mass withdrawal of countries, is that it becomes a court where neutral countries without a history of major conflict remain, Tamer says.
"If all the African states withdraw down from the ICC, they will have no jurisdiction over any of the African states. If everyone from Europe pulls out, they'll have no jurisdiction," he said.
"The court becomes a lame duck."
However, the court could face a reversal of sanctions with a potential new US administration in 2028.

But the onus falls on its member states to protect the court, and how far they are willing to step up by setting up laws or providing the financial and technical workarounds for the court to function.
"This is uncharted territory," McIntyre said.
"We've not previously seen a US administration that is so openly hostile to the rules-based order, and so we don't know the extent to which the ICC can withstand these kinds of attacks.
"It really comes down to the member states themselves setting up mechanisms through their own domestic legislation or through EU law to protect the institution."

The potential collapse of the institution though, would mean losing a crucial avenue for justice for victims of atrocities — as the court is one of the few bodies able to prosecute presidents, military commanders and leaders for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
"We (would) live in a world where the worst criminals will not face consequences for their actions," McIntyre said.
"A world of impunity."
